fixes.explanation: The church settling it together isn't Paul's reason here. He says he didn't want to act without consent "…so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will." (Philemon 1:14). The choice is Philemon's. Paul wants it to come from him.

Paul, who is writing this letter, opens with "…a prisoner of Christ Jesus…" Before he asks for anything, he tells Philemon right where he's sitting. I think that sets a humble tone for everything that follows. Nobody gets a more honest introduction than that.
Verse 2 says "…the church that meets at your house…" That means Philemon's house. Believers gathered at home. I hope Philemon owned enough chairs, friend.
A synagogue isn't mentioned in this letter. Paul writes to "…the church that meets at your house…" (Philemon 1:2). So the meeting place is Philemon's home. That's a church at a house.

Paul says he hears about "…your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints." That's the news that reaches him. Faith toward Jesus and love toward God's people, side by side. Good news travels, friend, even to a man in chains.

Gifts to the poor and the widows aren't what Paul mentions here. He says he hears about "…your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints." (Philemon 1:5). Two items on the list, and neither one is a donation receipt.
Insist is close in feeling to ordering, and that's the road Paul leaves alone. In verse 9 he says, "I prefer to appeal on the basis of love." The word is appeal, and love is the basis.

Sickness isn't part of this letter. Paul says, "Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me." (Philemon 1:11). The change is from useless to useful. Sick to healthy isn't the move Paul describes.

That statement matches what Paul says. He writes, "So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me." So the answer is True. Paul asks that Onesimus get the welcome Paul would get.

Paul says, "But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account." He's offering to cover it if there's anything owed. I think that's a lot of love for one letter. A man in chains offering to pay the tab if there is one.
Paul doesn't say friends. He writes, "…charge it to my account." (Philemon 1:18). If Onesimus owes anything, Paul offers to cover it himself. He's not passing the bill around.
Paul doesn't send the bill to the church. He writes, "…charge it to my account." (Philemon 1:18). If there's anything owed, Paul offers to put it on his own account. He steps up himself.

Paul writes, "Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings…" That's the title the text gives him. Paul passes his greetings along so Philemon hears from him. I think a hello from a fellow prisoner means a lot.

Paul doesn't call Epaphras a messenger here. He says, "Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings…" (Philemon 1:23). Epaphras is the one Paul calls his fellow prisoner. That's the title the text gives him.

Paul doesn't call Epaphras a host. He says, "Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings…" (Philemon 1:23). Paul calls him his fellow prisoner. No journey is mentioned here, friend.
